Cornelius Van Til
kor-NEEL-yus van TIL
proper noun (figure)
Cornelius Van Til (1895-1987), Dutch-American Reformed theologian and apologist. Cornelius (Latin, a Roman gens name; cf. Acts 10); Van Til, a Dutch surname ("from Til").

See also: Cornelius Van Til

📖 Biblical Definition

Cornelius Van Til (1895-1987) was the Dutch-American Reformed theologian who developed presuppositional apologetics — the method of defending the Christian faith that begins from the presupposition of the triune God and the authority of Scripture rather than from supposedly neutral common ground. Born in the Netherlands and raised in a Dutch Reformed immigrant family in America, Van Til was shaped by the Dutch neo-Calvinist tradition of Kuyper and Bavinck. He taught apologetics at Westminster Theological Seminary from its founding (1929) for over forty years. His central conviction was that there is no neutral ground between the believer and the unbeliever: every human being reasons from ultimate commitments, and the unbeliever, while suppressing the truth (Rom 1:18), still depends on the God he denies for the very rationality, logic, and moral order he uses to argue against Him. Van Til therefore rejected the "classical" and "evidentialist" apologetic methods that begin from neutral reason or brute facts and reason up to God; he argued instead that the Christian must challenge the unbeliever's whole worldview, showing that only the Christian worldview, with the self-attesting triune God and His revelation, provides the necessary foundation for reason, science, logic, and ethics — the "transcendental" argument. His thought, dense and demanding, shaped a major stream of Reformed apologetics through students and successors like Greg Bahnsen and John Frame. The dictionary registers that Reformed apologists debate presuppositionalism versus classical method; Van Til's enduring contribution is the insistence that apologetics must be God-centered and Scripture-governed, never conceding a supposedly neutral autonomy to fallen human reason.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Dutch-American Reformed theologian and apologist (1895-1987); developer of presuppositional apologetics; longtime Westminster Seminary professor; argued there is no neutral ground, and that only the triune God and His revelation ground reason, logic, and ethics.

CORNELIUS VAN TIL, proper noun. Dutch-American Reformed theologian and apologist (1895-1987).

Shaped by the Dutch neo-Calvinism of Kuyper and Bavinck; taught apologetics at Westminster Seminary 40+ years.

Developer of presuppositional apologetics: begin from the triune God and Scripture's authority, not from neutral common ground.

Argued there is no neutral ground; the unbeliever suppresses the truth (Rom 1:18) yet depends on the God he denies for rationality itself.

The transcendental argument: only the Christian worldview grounds reason, logic, science, and ethics. Influenced Bahnsen and Frame.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Cornelius Van Til is corrupted when presuppositionalism is caricatured as fideism or circular reasoning, when his rejection of neutral ground is misread as a refusal to give reasons, or when the apologetic-method debate is treated as a test of orthodoxy rather than a genuine intramural Reformed discussion.

expand to see more

Fideism-and-circularity caricature. Critics charge that presuppositionalism is mere fideism (believe without reasons) or viciously circular (assume God to prove God). Van Til's actual argument is the transcendental one: not "assume God, therefore God," but "the very preconditions of rational thought — logic, the uniformity of nature, moral absolutes — are intelligible only on the Christian worldview, and the unbeliever who uses them is borrowing from the God he denies." This is an argument, not a refusal to argue, and the "circularity" involved is the unavoidable circularity of all ultimate-authority claims (the classicalist's appeal to reason is equally self-referential at the foundation). The caricature mistakes a sophisticated argument for an evasion.

Method-as-orthodoxy-test misreading. The debate between presuppositional and classical/evidentialist apologetics is a genuine intramural discussion among Reformed Christians who share the same confession. Some on each side have treated their method as a test of orthodoxy, dismissing the other as compromised. The dictionary holds that both presuppositionalists (Van Til, Bahnsen, Frame) and classical apologists (the Old Princeton tradition, modern figures like Sproul) are within Reformed orthodoxy, debating method, not the faith itself. Van Til's enduring and widely-shared contribution is the insistence — against any method — that apologetics be God-centered and Scripture-governed, never conceding autonomous neutrality to fallen reason.
